title: Between the lines
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: LITOTES IS UNDERSTATEMENT THAT MEANS MORE, NOT LESS. nōn male is not 'not badly' but 'RATHER WELL' — a compliment — and nōn ignōrō is not 'I am not ignorant' but 'I know perfectly well'. L4-M5's haud sciō an was the extreme case, a litotes that reversed entirely, so this module COMPLETES the device rather than opening it: a learner who has met one will read the others correctly. And nōn bene is one word away from nōn male and really is criticism.

ignōrō IS THE EIGHTH WORD IN THIS COURSE WITH A NEGATIVE INSIDE IT, after nōlō, mālō, negō, nisi, nesciō, nōndum and nēmō. It is in- plus gnārus, 'not knowing'. By the fiftieth module that is a settled habit of the language — Latin prefers to weld a negative into a word than to put one beside it — and nōn ignōrō is therefore two negatives in one phrase that do NOT cancel, because the litotes is the point.

THE INDIRECT QUESTION ARRIVES AND IT IS THE LAST CONSTRUCTION THIS COURSE OWES. L4-M5's haud sciō an only looked like one. quaerō quid agās is 'I ask what you are doing' — with a SUBJUNCTIVE, where English keeps the indicative — and that single fact is the whole difference and the reason this waited for a level whose learner is fluent in the mood. quid agis? was L1-M2's greeting; quid agās inside a clause is a report, and the mood is the only change.

A LOADED QUESTION IS AN INDIRECT REQUEST, AND L4-M4 BUILT THE MACHINERY. nōnne expects yes, so nōnne mē adiuvābis? asks for help while handing the listener the easier answer — English does the same with a tag question. sī placet plus a subjunctive is the elaborate version. The course now has FOUR ways of asking for help: adiuvā, adiuvā quaesō, nōnne mē adiuvābis, sī placet mē adiuvēs — blunt to elaborate, in that order.

ONE MOOD, MANY MASTERS: S09 has two subjunctives for two unrelated reasons — quaerās because sī placet asks for it, agam because an indirect question demands it. Five conjunctions and two constructions now require the subjunctive (ut, nē, licet, an, cum, dōnec, plus a question inside a clause and a wish with nothing in front of it), and a single sentence can easily carry two of them for reasons that have nothing to do with each other.

SARCASM IS M2's DEVICE IN A COLDER REGISTER, and this module does not repeat that one. M2 teased a friend; here the listener is meant to work something out and possibly resent it — and a litotes after a superlative is what tips the balance, because nobody understates what they actually admire. The same optimē carries both, and only the usage line tells them apart, which is the honest way to teach tone in a language nobody will hear you speak.

words.note: 'Not', in front of what it denies — and here it denies male, not the writing.
'Badly'. L1-M2's bene is its opposite, and with nōn in front of it — nōn male — it means 'rather well', which is understatement rather than denial.
'You write' — scrībō, scrībis, scrībit, scrīpsī. L1-M6's verb.

words.note: 'Not', in front of ignōrō.
'I do not know' — in- plus gnārus, so the negative is inside the word. The EIGHTH such word in this course, and nōn ignōrō means 'I know perfectly well'.
'Why' — L1-M9's question word, and here it opens an indirect question like quid does.
'Not', and here it is inside the reported question: why you are NOT coming.

sentences.trap: Two negatives and they do not cancel, because they are in different clauses. nōn ignōrō is a litotes meaning 'I know perfectly well' and nōn veniās is the content of what is known — which is M5's two-clause rule arriving inside a construction rather than across a sentence.

words.note: 'If' — a politeness frame here rather than a condition.
'It pleases' — impersonal. sī placet is 'please' at its most formal.
'That you may ask' — the present subjunctive of quaerō, which sī placet requires.
'What', opening an indirect question.
'That I may do' — the present subjunctive of agō, reported about the speaker.
'Not', in front of male.
'Badly'. L1-M2's bene is its opposite, and with nōn in front of it — nōn male — it means 'rather well', which is understatement rather than denial.
'For' — and it comes SECOND in its clause, never first. L1-M10's word.
'I wrote' — the perfect of scrībō. L1-M6's verb.

sentences.trap: TWO SUBJUNCTIVES FOR TWO DIFFERENT REASONS: quaerās because sī placet asks for it, agam because an indirect question demands it. The mood is not doing one job in Latin — five conjunctions and two constructions now require it — and a single sentence can carry two of them for unrelated reasons.

sentences.trap: Nothing in this sentence says what it means. A litotes claims knowledge by denying ignorance; a loaded question asks for help by expecting agreement; a politeness frame asks for attention by not asking. Three indirect moves, four subjunctives, and every word of it taught — which is what 'between the lines' means when a language has no tone of voice on the page.
sentences.sound: Twenty-five syllables in three moves. Read it as three, and not one of them is literal.
